intro: This branch describes curves in two new ways: by tracking a moving point over time (parametric), or by angle and distance from a center (polar). Calculus then finds slopes, lengths and areas for them.

VI.8.01.what: A parametric curve gives x and y each as a formula in time, like tracing the path of a moving bug.

levels.a: Reads a curve given as separate formulas for x and y in terms of time.
levels.b: Plots the curve from a table of time values.
levels.c: Marks the direction the point moves along the curve.
levels.d: Writes parametric formulas for circles and ellipses.

VI.8.02.what: Removing the time variable to get an ordinary equation linking x and y directly.

levels.a: Solves one formula for time and substitutes into the other.
levels.b: Uses a trig identity to remove time from sine and cosine formulas.
levels.c: Notices when only part of the ordinary graph is actually traced.
levels.d: Compares the parametric graph with the ordinary one.

VI.8.03.what: Finding the slope of a parametric curve by dividing how fast y changes by how fast x changes.

levels.a: Uses the formula: rate of y over rate of x.
levels.b: Writes tangent lines to parametric curves.
levels.c: Finds points where the curve has a flat tangent.
levels.d: Finds points where the curve has a vertical tangent.

VI.8.04.what: Finding how the slope of a parametric curve changes, which tells which way it bends.

levels.a: States the formula for the second derivative.
levels.b: Computes it for a given curve.
levels.c: Uses it to decide which way the curve bends.
levels.d: Avoids the common mistake of just differentiating the slope in time.

VI.8.05.what: Finding the length of a parametric curve, like the distance a moving point travels.

levels.a: States the arc length formula for parametric curves.
levels.d: Finds the total distance traveled by a moving point.

VI.8.06.what: Describing motion in two dimensions, like a thrown ball, using arrows (vectors) for position, velocity and acceleration.

levels.a: Writes position as an arrow from the origin (a position vector).
levels.d: Models the curved paths of thrown objects.

VI.8.07.what: Polar coordinates locate a point by its distance from the center and its angle, like giving directions by compass bearing and distance.

levels.a: Plots points given as a distance and an angle.
levels.b: Converts polar points to ordinary x and y coordinates.
levels.d: Recognizes that one point has many different polar names.

VI.8.08.what: Sketching curves described in polar form, which produces shapes like flowers, hearts and spirals.

levels.c: Graphs heart-shaped cardioids and looped limaçons.

VI.8.09.what: Finding the slope of a polar curve at a point.

levels.a: Rewrites a polar curve as a parametric curve.
levels.b: Uses the slope formula for polar curves.
levels.c: Finds tangent lines where the curve passes through the center.
levels.d: Finds flat and vertical tangent points.

VI.8.10.what: Finding the area inside a polar curve by adding up thin pizza-slice wedges.

levels.a: Uses the wedge formula: half the integral of r squared.
levels.b: Finds the area of one petal of a rose.
levels.c: Finds the correct angles where the curve passes through the center.
levels.d: Uses symmetry to simplify the calculation.

VI.8.11.what: Finding the area between two polar curves.

levels.a: Finds where the two curves meet.
levels.b: Subtracts the inner curve's area from the outer one's.

VI.8.12.what: Finding the length of a polar curve.

levels.a: States the polar arc length formula.
levels.d: Estimates it with technology when no exact answer is possible.
